report:
### Conclusion
The claim that prolonged use of cloth or surgical face masks causes dangerous carbon-dioxide ($CO_2$) buildup (hypercapnia) is supported neither by major public health organizations nor clinical evidence. While gas rebreathing has been debated in some scoping reviews, standard medical consensus confirms that cloth and surgical masks allow carbon dioxide molecules to freely diffuse through the material.

### Evidence Behind the Health Claim

1. **World Health Organization (WHO)**: The WHO explicitly debunks the claim, confirming that proper use of medical masks does not cause carbon dioxide intoxication or oxygen deficiency (https://www.who.int/emergencies/diseases/novel-coronavirus-2019/advice-for-public/myth-busters).
2. **Clinical Research**: A study published in the *Annals of the American Thoracic Society* evaluated gas exchange in individuals wearing masks—including patients with severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)—and found that face masks are unlikely to cause $CO_2$ overexposure or retention (https://www.newswise.com/coronavirus/face-masks-unlikely-to-cause-over-exposure-to-carbon-dioxide-even-in-patients-with-lung-disease).
3. **Medical Consensus and Real-World Use**: Health systems, such as Michigan Medicine, note that healthcare workers routinely wear surgical masks for extended periods during long procedures without experiencing $CO_2$ toxicity or adverse events (https://www.michiganmedicine.org/health-lab/4-mask-myths-put-you-risk). 
4. **Fact-Checking Findings**: Associated Press reports confirm there is no scientific evidence that wearing a cloth or surgical mask poses a risk of hypercapnia or dangerous $CO_2$ accumulation in the bloodstream (https://apnews.com/article/archive-fact-checking-9101740032).

Carbon dioxide gas molecules are significantly smaller than the weave of cloth or surgical mask fibers, allowing exhalation products to pass out easily while providing a barrier against larger respiratory droplets.
